issues.legal_issue: A surrender of a widow’s entire estate accelerates succession only if it amounts to complete self-effacement with respect to the whole estate.
material_facts: The widow’s 1906 transfer reserved to her cultivating rights over 91.5 acres, an area the Court regarded as substantial.
A later transfer of those lands on similar terms did not cure the absence of a complete surrender.
The appeal challenged the finding that the transactions did not accelerate succession.
issues.conclusion: There was no valid surrender or acceleration of succession; the transactions were gifts that could operate only during the transferor’s lifetime.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle that surrender accelerates succession only when the widow completely effaces herself with respect to the whole estate; partial self-effacement is not a valid surrender. The Court cited no earlier cases or statutory provisions for this principle.

predicates.appeal_challenges_surrender_validity: The proceeding is an appeal that challenges whether a transfer constituted a valid surrender.
predicates.transferor_retained_substantial_estate_p: The transferor reserved substantial property or rights in the estate for herself.
predicates.surrender_did_not_cover_whole_estate: The transferor did not completely withdraw from the whole estate.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a surrender and the transferor retained substantial property because the surrender did not cover the whole estate, the surrender is invalid and succession is not accelerated.

issues.legal_issue: When a surrender has not accelerated succession, a claim by a reversioner is not barred by adverse possession that began before the estate vested in the reversioners.
material_facts: Because there was no valid surrender, the estate vested in the nearest reversioners only when the widow died.
The trial court had found that the opposing claimants were in adverse possession from the widow’s death in 1927.
The suit was brought within a few months of the widow’s death.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not barred by limitation because succession had not vested before the widow’s death and the suit was brought within a few months thereafter.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that, absent a valid surrender, succession to the estate vested in the nearest reversioners only on the widow’s death; adverse possession could not bar their claim before that vesting. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited on this point.

predicates.reversionary_estate_claim: The claimant seeks an estate as a reversioner.
predicates.no_valid_surrender_preceded_vesting: No valid surrender caused the estate to vest in the reversioners before the life holder died.
predicates.suit_filed_within_months_after_vesting: The claimant filed suit within a few months after the estate vested in the reversioners.

issues.definition: A reversionary claim is not barred by limitation when no valid surrender preceded vesting and suit is filed within a few months after vesting.

issues.legal_issue: Costs may be withheld from successful respondents when the circumstances of the appeal make an award of costs unnecessary.
material_facts: The appellant’s advocate had difficulty explaining the practical advantage of success in light of legislation under which some properties might have vested in the State.
The respondents’ advocate left the question of costs to the Court’s discretion.
issues.conclusion: The appeal was dismissed without costs in the Supreme Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court exercised its discretion over costs in light of the circumstances and the respondents’ position. No statutory provision or earlier case was cited.

predicates.practical_benefit_of_success_unclear: The appellant cannot clearly explain the practical benefit that success in the appeal would provide.
predicates.respondents_leave_costs_to_court: The respondents leave the question of costs to the court’s discretion.

issues.definition: When an appeal is dismissed, the practical benefit of success is unclear, and respondents leave costs to the court, the court awards them no costs.
